title: Part 1, Chapter 30
paragraphs: About the cleverness shown by the fair Dorothea, with other pleasant and entertaining matters

The curate had hardly finished speaking when Sancho said, "On my faith, then, señor licentiate, the one who did that deed was my master; and it wasn't for lack of my warning him beforehand and telling him to be careful, that it was a sin to set them free, since they were all on the march there because they were special scoundrels."

"Blockhead!" said Don Quixote at this. "It is no business or concern of knights-errant to inquire whether the persons in distress, chained, or oppressed whom they meet on the high roads go that way and suffer in that condition because of their faults or because of their misfortunes. The only thing that concerns us is to help them as people in need, with regard to their suffering and not to their crimes. I came across a chaplet — a string of miserable, unfortunate people — and did for them what my sense of duty demands, and as for the rest, let it be as it may. Whoever objects to it — saving the sacred dignity of the señor licentiate and his honoured person — I say he knows little about chivalry and lies like a whoreson villain, and I will make him understand this to the fullest extent with my sword." And with that he settled himself in his stirrups and pressed down his morion — for the barber's basin, which to him was Mambrino's helmet, he carried hanging at the saddle-bow until he could repair the damage the galley slaves had done to it.

Dorothea, who was shrewd and quick-witted, by now thoroughly understood Don Quixote's crazy turn and that everyone except Sancho Panza was playing along; so as not to be outdone, when she saw his irritation she said to him, "Sir Knight, remember the favour you have promised me, and that under its terms you must not engage in any other adventure, however urgent. Calm yourself; if the licentiate had known that the galley slaves had been set free by that unconquered arm, he would have sewed up his mouth three times over, or even bitten his tongue three times before he said a word that smacked of disrespect to your worship."
"That I swear heartily," said the curate, "and I would even have plucked out a whisker of my moustache."

"I will hold my peace, señora," said Don Quixote, "and curb the natural anger that had risen in my chest, and I will proceed in peace and quiet until I have fulfilled my promise. But in return for this restraint I entreat you to tell me — if you have no objection — what is the nature of your trouble, and how many, who, and what kind of persons they are from whom I am to demand satisfaction and on whom I am to take vengeance on your behalf."
"I'll do that with all my heart," replied Dorothea, "if it doesn't tire you to listen to miseries and misfortunes."

"It will not tire me, señora," said Don Quixote. To which Dorothea replied, "Well, if that's so, give me your attention." As soon as she said this, Cardenio and the barber drew close to her side, eager to hear what kind of story the quick-witted Dorothea would invent for herself; and Sancho did the same, for he was as much taken in by her as his master. She settled herself comfortably in the saddle, and with the help of a few coughs and other preliminaries to give herself time to think, she began with great spirit in this fashion.

"First of all, sirs, I would have you know that my name is —" and here she stopped for a moment, because she'd forgotten the name the curate had given her. But he came to her rescue, seeing her difficulty, and said, "It's no wonder, señora, that your highness should be confused and embarrassed when telling the tale of your misfortunes; such afflictions often have the effect of depriving the sufferers of memory, so that they cannot even remember their own names, as is the case now with your ladyship, who has forgotten that she is called the Princess Micomicona, lawful heiress of the great kingdom of Micomicon. With this cue your highness may now recall to your sorrowful memory everything you wish to tell us."

"That is the truth," said the damsel, "but I think from here on I shall need no further prompting, and I shall bring my true story safely into port. Here it is. The king my father, who was called Tinacrio the Sapient, was very learned in what they call the magic arts, and by his craft he became aware that my mother, who was called Queen Jaramilla, was to die before he did, and that soon after he too was to depart this life, and I would be left an orphan without father or mother. But all this, he declared, did not grieve or distress him as much as the certain knowledge that a prodigious giant — the lord of a great island close to our kingdom, Pandafilando of the Scowl by name (for it's said that, although his eyes are properly placed and straight, he always looks sideways as if he squinted, and he does it out of malice, to strike fear and terror into those he looks at) — that he knew, I say, that this giant, on becoming aware of my orphaned condition, would overrun my kingdom with a mighty force and strip me of everything, not leaving me even a small village to shelter in; but that I could avoid all this ruin and misfortune if I were willing to marry him. However, as far as he could see, he never expected me to consent to such an unequal marriage; and he spoke no more than the truth in this, since it has never entered my mind to marry that giant, or any other, however great or enormous he may be. My father said, too, that when he was dead and I saw Pandafilando about to invade my kingdom, I was not to wait and try to defend myself, for that would be the ruin of me; instead I should leave the kingdom entirely open to him if I wished to avoid the death and total destruction of my good and loyal vassals, since there would be no way of defending myself against the giant's devilish power. He told me I should at once set out with some of my followers for Spain, where I would find relief in my distress on finding a certain knight-errant whose fame by then would extend over the whole kingdom, and who would be called, if I remember rightly, Don Azote or Don Gigote."
"He must have said 'Don Quixote,' señora," Sancho put in at this, "otherwise known as the Knight of the Rueful Countenance."

"That's it," said Dorothea. "He said, moreover, that the knight would be tall of stature and lank of feature; and that on his right side under the left shoulder, or thereabouts, he would have a grey mole with hairs like bristles."
On hearing this, Don Quixote said to his squire, "Here, Sancho my son, lend a hand and help me strip, because I want to see if I'm the knight that sage king foretold."
"What does your worship want to strip for?" said Dorothea.
"To see if I have the mole your father spoke of," answered Don Quixote.
"There's no need to strip," said Sancho. "I know your worship has just such a mole in the middle of your backbone, which is the mark of a strong man."

"That's enough," said Dorothea. "With friends we must not look too closely into trifles, and whether it's on the shoulder or on the backbone matters little; what counts is that there's a mole, wherever it may be, since it's all the same flesh. No doubt my good father hit the truth in every particular, and I have made a lucky hit in commending myself to Don Quixote — for he is the one my father spoke of, since the features of his face correspond with those given to this knight by that wide fame he has earned not only in Spain but in all La Mancha. I had hardly landed at Osuna when I heard such accounts of his exploits that at once my heart told me he was the very one I had come in search of."
"But how did you land at Osuna, señora," asked Don Quixote, "when it's not a seaport?"
Before Dorothea could reply, the curate cut in and said, "The princess means that after she had landed at Málaga, the first place where she heard of your worship was Osuna."
"That is what I meant to say," said Dorothea.
"And that would be only natural," said the curate. "Will your majesty please go on?"

"There's nothing more to add," said Dorothea, "except that in finding Don Quixote I have had such good fortune that I already count and consider myself queen and mistress of all my domains, since out of his courtesy and magnanimity he has granted me the favour of accompanying me wherever I may lead him — which will be only to bring him face to face with Pandafilando of the Scowl, so that he may kill him and restore to me what has been unjustly taken from me. All this must come about satisfactorily, since my good father Tinacrio the Sapient foretold it; he also left it stated in writing, in Chaldee or Greek characters (for I cannot read them), that if this predicted knight, after cutting the giant's throat, should be willing to marry me, I was to offer myself at once without protest as his lawful wife, and yield him possession of my kingdom together with my person."
"What do you think now, friend Sancho?" said Don Quixote at this. "Do you hear that? Didn't I tell you so? Look — we already have a kingdom to govern and a queen to marry!"

"On my oath that's so," said Sancho, "and bad luck to anyone who won't marry after slitting Señor Pandahilado's windpipe! And then, how ill-favoured the queen is! I wish the fleas in my bed were that kind!"

And with that he cut a couple of capers in the air with every sign of extreme satisfaction, then ran to seize the bridle of Dorothea's mule, and pulling it up he fell on his knees before her, begging her to give him her hand to kiss in acknowledgement that he accepted her as his queen and mistress. Which of the bystanders could have helped laughing to see the madness of the master and the simplicity of the servant? Dorothea therefore gave him her hand and promised to make him a great lord in her kingdom, when Heaven should be good enough to allow her to recover and enjoy it; for which Sancho returned his thanks in words that set them all laughing again.

"This, sirs," Dorothea continued, "is my story. It only remains to tell you that of all the attendants I took with me from my kingdom, I have none left except this well-bearded squire, for all the others were drowned in a great tempest we encountered when in sight of port. He and I came to land on a couple of planks as if by a miracle; and indeed the whole course of my life is a miracle and a mystery, as you may have noticed. If I have been over-detailed about any of it, or not as precise as I should have been, blame it on what the licentiate said at the beginning of my tale — that constant and excessive troubles deprive the sufferers of their memory."

"They shall not deprive me of mine, exalted and worthy princess," said Don Quixote, "however great and unparalleled those I endure in your service may be. Here I confirm anew the favour I have promised you, and I swear to go with you to the ends of the earth until I find myself in the presence of your fierce enemy, whose haughty head I trust by the strength of my arm to cut off with the edge of this — I will not say good sword, thanks to Ginés de Pasamonte who carried off mine" — (this he muttered between his teeth, and then went on) — "and when it has been cut off and you have been put in peaceful possession of your realm, it shall be left to your own decision to dispose of your person as may please you most; for so long as my memory is occupied, my will enslaved, and my understanding enthralled by her — I say no more — it's impossible for me even for a moment to contemplate marriage, even with a Phoenix."
His master's last words about not wanting to marry were so disagreeable to Sancho that, raising his voice, he exclaimed with great irritation:

"By my oath, Señor Don Quixote, you are not in your right senses; how can your worship possibly refuse to marry such an exalted princess as this? Do you think Fortune will offer you behind every stone a piece of luck like this one? Is my lady Dulcinea more beautiful, perhaps? Not she; not half as beautiful; I'll even go so far as to say she doesn't come up to the shoe of this one here. A poor chance I have of getting that county I'm waiting for, if your worship goes hunting for delicacies at the bottom of the sea. In the devil's name, marry, marry, and take this kingdom that comes to hand without any trouble; and when you're king, make me a marquis or governor of a province, and the rest can go to the devil."

When Don Quixote heard such blasphemies uttered against his lady Dulcinea, he could not bear it, and lifting his pike, without saying anything to Sancho or uttering a word, he gave him two such whacks that he knocked him to the ground; and if Dorothea hadn't shouted at him to spare him, he would no doubt have taken his life on the spot.

"Do you think," he said to him after a pause, "you scurvy clown, that you are always to be interfering with me, and that you are always to be giving offence and I always to be pardoning? Don't get any such idea, you impious scoundrel — for that's beyond all doubt what you are, since you've set your tongue going against the peerless Dulcinea. Don't you know, you lout, vagabond, beggar, that were it not for the strength she pours into my arm I wouldn't have the power to kill a flea? Tell me, scoffer with a viper's tongue, what do you think has won this kingdom and cut off this giant's head and made you a marquis (for I count all this as already done and decided) but the might of Dulcinea, using my arm as the instrument of her achievements? She fights in me and conquers in me, and I live and breathe in her, and owe my life and being to her. O whoreson scoundrel, how ungrateful you are! You see yourself raised from the dust of the earth to be a titled lord, and the return you make for so great a benefit is to speak ill of her who has conferred it on you!"
Sancho was not so stunned that he didn't hear everything his master said, and getting up with some quickness he ran to place himself behind Dorothea's palfrey, and from there he said to his master:

"Tell me, señor — if your worship is resolved not to marry this great princess, it's plain the kingdom won't be yours; and if it's not, how can you bestow favours on me? That's what I complain of. Let your worship at any rate marry this queen, now that we have her here as if showered down from heaven, and afterwards you can go back to my lady Dulcinea; there must have been kings in the world who kept mistresses. As to beauty, I have nothing to do with that; to tell the truth, I like them both, though I have never seen the lady Dulcinea."
"What? Never seen her, you blasphemous traitor!" exclaimed Don Quixote. "Didn't you just now bring me a message from her?"
"I mean," said Sancho, "that I did not see her at such leisure that I could take particular notice of her beauty, or of her charms piece by piece; but taken in the lump, I like her."
"Now I forgive you," said Don Quixote, "and you forgive me the injury I have done you, for our first impulses are not in our control."
"That I see," replied Sancho, "and with me the wish to speak is always the first impulse, and I cannot help saying, at least once, whatever's on the tip of my tongue."
"All the same, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "watch what you say, because the pitcher goes so often to the well — I need say no more."
"Well, well," said Sancho, "God is in heaven, and he sees all the tricks, and will judge who does more harm — me by not speaking right, or your worship by not doing it."

"That's enough," said Dorothea. "Run, Sancho, kiss your lord's hand and beg his pardon, and from now on be more careful with your praise and abuse; and say nothing in disparagement of that lady of El Toboso, of whom I know nothing except that I am her servant. Put your trust in God, and you'll not fail to obtain some position that will let you live like a prince."

Sancho came forward hanging his head and begged his master's hand, which Don Quixote presented with dignity, giving him his blessing as soon as he had kissed it. He then told him to come on ahead a little, as he had questions to ask and matters of great importance to discuss with him. Sancho obeyed, and when the two had gone some distance ahead, Don Quixote said to him, "Since your return I have had no opportunity or time to ask you many particulars concerning your mission and the answer you brought back; now that chance has granted us the time and opportunity, don't deny me the happiness you can give me with such good news."
"Let your worship ask whatever you want," answered Sancho, "and I'll find a way out of all of it, as I found a way in; but I beg you, señor, not to be so vengeful in future."
"Why do you say that, Sancho?" said Don Quixote.

"I say it," he returned, "because those blows just now were more for the quarrel the devil stirred up between us the other night than for what I said against my lady Dulcinea, whom I love and revere as I would a relic — though there's nothing relic-like about her — merely as something belonging to your worship."
"Say no more on that subject, for your life, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "for it displeases me. I have already pardoned you for it, and you know the common saying, 'for a fresh sin a fresh penance.'"

While this was going on they saw, coming along the road they were following, a man mounted on an ass. When he came close he seemed to be a gypsy; but Sancho Panza, whose eyes and heart were wherever he saw asses, had no sooner laid eyes on the man than he knew him for Ginés de Pasamonte; and by the thread of the gypsy he got at the ball — his ass. For it was, in fact, Dapple who was carrying Pasamonte, who to escape recognition and sell the ass had disguised himself as a gypsy, being able to speak the gypsy language, and many others, as well as if they were his own. Sancho saw him and recognised him, and the instant he did so he shouted at him, "Ginesillo, you thief, give up my treasure, release my life, don't trouble yourself with my repose, leave my ass, leave my delight, get out, scoundrel, get gone, thief, and give back what isn't yours!"

There was no need for so many words or curses, for at the first one Ginés jumped down, and at a sprinter's pace made off and got clear of them all. Sancho hurried to his Dapple, and embracing him said, "How have you been, my treasure, Dapple of my eyes, my comrade?" — all the while kissing him and caressing him as if he were a human being. The ass held his peace, and let himself be kissed and caressed by Sancho without answering a single word. The others all came up and congratulated him on having found Dapple, Don Quixote especially, who told him that despite this he would not cancel the order for the three ass-colts; for which Sancho thanked him.

While the two had been going along talking like this, the curate remarked to Dorothea that she had shown great cleverness, both in the story itself and in its conciseness, and in how closely it resembled the kind found in the books of chivalry. She said she had often amused herself reading them, but that she didn't know the location of the provinces or seaports, and so she had said at random that she had landed at Osuna.

"So I saw," said the curate, "and that's why I made haste to say what I did, by which it was all set right. But isn't it a strange thing to see how readily this unhappy gentleman believes all these fictions and lies, simply because they're in the style and manner of the absurdities in his books?"
"It is," said Cardenio, "and so uncommon and unparalleled that if anyone tried to invent and concoct it as fiction, I doubt there's any wit keen enough to imagine it."

"But another strange thing about it," said the curate, "is that, apart from the silly things this worthy gentleman says in connection with his obsession, on any other subject he can discuss things in a perfectly rational way, showing that his mind is quite clear and composed. So provided his chivalry is not touched on, no one would take him for anything but a man of thoroughly sound understanding."
While they were having this conversation, Don Quixote continued his with Sancho, saying:

"Friend Panza, let's forgive and forget our quarrels, and now tell me, putting aside any anger or irritation, where, how, and when did you find Dulcinea? What was she doing? What did you say to her? What did she answer? How did she look when she was reading my letter? Who copied it out for you? — and everything in the matter that seems to you worth knowing, asking, and learning. Neither add to it nor falsify to please me, nor cut it short and deprive me of any of it."
"Señor," replied Sancho, "if the truth is to be told, nobody copied out the letter for me, because I carried no letter at all."

"It's as you say," said Don Quixote, "for the notebook in which I wrote it I found in my own possession two days after you left, which gave me very great vexation, since I had no idea what you would do on finding yourself without any letter; I felt sure you would come back from the spot where you first noticed it was missing."

"I should have done that," said Sancho, "if I hadn't got it by heart when your worship read it to me — so that I repeated it to a sacristan, who copied it out from hearing it, so exactly that he said in all the days of his life, though he had read many a letter of excommunication, he had never seen or read so pretty a letter as that one."
"And have you got it still in your memory, Sancho?" said Don Quixote.

"No, señor," replied Sancho, "because as soon as I had repeated it, seeing there was no further use for it, I set about forgetting it; and if I recall any of it, it's that bit about 'Scrubbing' — I mean to say 'Sovereign Lady' — and the end, 'Yours till death, the Knight of the Rueful Countenance;' and between those two I put more than three hundred 'my souls' and 'my life's' and 'my eyes.'"
